data.title: Top UN Court Finds Myanmar Guilty Of Genocide Against Rohingya
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - The International Court of Justice has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority during military operations in Rakhine State in the last decade. It is the first time the UN's top court has found a state responsible for genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention.

At the end of a three-hour ruling at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, President Yuji Iwasawa also declared that Myanmar had failed to prevent and punish genocide, after detailing how the eastern Asian country's military had perpetrated 'extreme violence' against mainly Muslim Rohingya communities in Rakhine state.

The ruling establishes that Myanmar's security forces and other State organs intentionally committed specifically prohibited acts covered by Article II of the Genocide Convention.

The ICJ ruling came after studying graphic evidence and testimonies provided by survivors and reports from international investigators describing how Rohingya villages and bridges had been set alight and bulldozed, with men and boys executed and girls and women raped during military clearance operations in northern Rakhine in 2017.

The military clearance operations also involved the murder of infants, which 'supports the inference that Myanmar's security forces acted with the intent to prevent births among the group,' Judge Iwasawa added.

Delivering the court's ruling, the ICJ President described how the mainly Muslim Rohingya living in Rakhine state in western Myanmar had been the target of successive clearance operations by the State military, after decades of intercommunal violence.

The 2017 clearance operations prompted widespread international condemnation after some 700,000 Rohingya fled northern Rakhine state across the border to Bangladesh.

According to the court, an estimated 10,000 Rohingya were killed during the clearance operations, citing supporting evidence.

A separate study estimated that the military and the local Rakhine population killed at least 25,000 Rohingya people.

The case at the ICJ was initiated by The Gambia in November 2019. It has become one of the most closely watched proceedings before the world's highest court.

The Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim ethnic minority in western Myanmar's Rakhine State, were stripped of citizenship under the 1982 Citizenship Law and have faced decades of state discrimination, movement restrictions, and abuse.

More than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh during the 2017 crisis, adding to roughly one million Rohingya refugees living in Bangladeshi camps.

Since 2024, fighting in Rakhine State involving Myanmar's military and the Arakan Army has continued to endanger Rohingya civilians.

The court heard that nearly 400 villages - approximately 40 per cent of the almost 1,000 villages in the three townships of northern Rakhine state - were partially or totally destroyed during and after the 2017 clearance operations.

Myanmar's authorities have consistently denied committing genocide, arguing that military 'clearance operations' were counterterrorism actions responding to attacks by armed groups such as the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The ICJ rejected that defense, finding that the military failed to distinguish between militants and civilians

The Court ordered the government of Myanmar to enact legislation giving full effect to its obligations under the Genocide Convention; to take immediate steps to investigate all persons suspected of having committed acts contrary to the Convention and, if warranted, to prosecute and punish them.

In addition, the ruling orders Myanmar to provide guarantee that such violence is not repeated in the future.

Finally, the Court decided that Myanmar should transmit to it within two years a report on the measures of restitution it has adopted and the amount and modalities of compensation.

The judgment is binding on the parties to the case and without appeal.

UN leadership, human rights organizations, and several governments welcomed the judgment as a milestone for accountability.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres welcomed the judgment as a 'powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide. It is a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand.'

data.title: Asia spot prices fall to 6-week low on weak demand, improved supplies
data.description:
By Emily Chow

Asia spot liquefied natural gas prices slipped for a third consecutive week, weighed down by weaker demand and comfortable inventories in Asia, and improved supplies from the Strait of Hormuz and the US.

The average price for January delivery into northeast Asia (LNG-AS) was estimated at $26.90 per million British thermal units (mmBtu) this week, down from $31.30/mmBtu the previous week and the lowest since October 9.

Continued LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz and comfortable Asian inventories that limit spot buying interest are easing market pressures, said Ole Dramdal, senior analyst at Rystad Energy.

Some buying interest, however, was visible in South and Southeast Asia, he said, with Thailand, Pakistan and Vietnam showing buying interest.

In northeast Asia, buyers have stepped back from the spot market, with Chinese firms purchasing only enough to meet storage targets, South Korean buyers already covered for winter, and Japanese demand well supplied by long-term contracts, said Martin Senior, head of LNG pricing at Argus.

"And at least four cargoes have diverted away from Egypt this week, prompting further immediate supply availability," he added.

"Egyptian demand has fallen as the nation has cut some fertiliser and industrial supply, and has increased fuel oil imports to replace some gas in power generation."

In Europe, S&P Global Commodity Insights assessed its daily Northwest Europe LNG price benchmark for cargoes delivered in December on an ex-ship basis at $26.765/mmBtu on Thursday, a discount of $0.53/mmBtu to the price at the Dutch TTF gas hub.

Spark Commodities assessed it at $26.572/mmBtu, while Argus assessed the January price at $26.65/mmBtu.

"European LNG prices declined sharply over the week as improving global supply expectations and weak Asian competition outweighed tightening European winter fundamentals," said Aly Blakeway, head of Atlantic LNG at S&P Global Energy, adding that US feedgas around record-high levels pointed to strong Atlantic Basin export availability.

"Middle Eastern supply also continued its gradual recovery. Qatar and Abu Dhabi exported around a cargo per day during the first half of November."

European gas markets, however, remain tight heading into year-end, with low storage levels leaving limited room to absorb additional shocks, said Hans van Cleef, head of energy research at EqoLibrium.

"Weather is the main short-term swing factor; an early cold spell would accelerate withdrawals and create chaos. The issues around the Strait of Hormuz remains the key geopolitical supply risk."

In LNG freight, Atlantic rates fell to $20,500 a day, while Pacific rates declined to $52,000 a day, said Spark Commodities analyst Qasim Afghan.

The US front-month arbitrage to northeast Asia via the Cape of Good Hope continues to point firmly to Europe, while the Nigerian prompt arbitrage, also via the Cape, is pointing to Europe for a fourth straight week, he added.

data.title: Bitcoin, Ether Edge Higher But Stay Near Multimonth Lows
data.description:
By Joe Stonor

Major cryptocurrencies edged higher Friday but failed to recover sharp losses from the last session as investors ditched risky assets.

Bitcoin was up 0.1% at $61,559 in early European trade, its lowest level since early July. Ether also rose but failed to significantly regain losses, adding 0.2% to $1,743.

Bitcoin fell sharply Thursday to trade close to $61,500, as Anthropic's IPO failed to spark a broader stock market rally. The cryptocurrency trades around 29% lower than its September peak.

Increased institutional adoption of digital assets is proving a near-term headwind for crypto assets, rather than a boon, said Nidal Abdel Hadi, chief executive of investment group Finoro. Higher correlation to stocks makes crypto more vulnerable to broader risk-off sentiment shifts.

"The provocative possibility is that bitcoin's integration into mainstream finance has weakened its ability to behave independently of traditional liquidity cycles," Hadi said.

For the day ahead, U.S. consumer sentiment data will help shape inflation expectations and, in turn, Federal Reserve policy. Expectations for increased Fed tightening are bearish for nonyielding digital assets.

data.title: INTERVIEW - European solar manufacturing needs stronger EU support, HoloSolis CEO says
data.description:
November 20 (Renewables Now) - French solar manufacturer HoloSolis is targeting the start of production at its planned 5-GW gigafactory in Hambach by late 2029 or early 2030, with its next fundraising round dependent on the adoption of sufficiently ambitious EU legislation to support European-made photovoltaic products.

In an interview with Renewables Now, the company's new CEO, Henri Poupart-Lafarge, discusses the project's financing and revised timeline, its strategy to build a European supply chain and the challenges of competing with established Asian manufacturers.

What is the current status of the Hambach gigafactory project and what are the remaining milestones before construction can begin?

HoloSolis has just closed its first fundraising round, securing EUR 15 million (USD 16.5m), and has been granted around EUR 400 million in public financing from both France and the EU.

The remaining milestones are to complete the detailed engineering (made possible by the EUR-15-million fundraising round), conclude the relevant grant agreements, advance the next financing steps, and complete procurement and construction preparations.

Previous statements indicated that construction would begin in 2027, with the first panels expected in 2028. Are these still your targets?

Before being able to finalise the next fundraising round, we need strong and ambitious regulation at the EU level through the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). This legislation is expected to be finalised next year. We will then be able to start fundraising for the construction of the first building by mid-2027. Construction will start in mid-2028, and production will begin at the end of 2029 or in early 2030.

Have you already secured agreements with potential customers for the factory’s future output?

We have secured letters of intent from customers covering more than 30 GW of production, representing strong commercial interest in the project. However, firm contracts will only be signed after the publication of the IAA, provided that the legislation is strong enough to recognise the value of European-made cells and modules.

How dependent will the gigafactory be on imported components and raw materials?

Our objective is to build a genuinely European industrial base for cells and modules, while being realistic about the current structure of global supply chains. Some upstream materials, specialised equipment and components will initially need to be sourced internationally because European capacity is not yet available at the required scale.

Our priority is to reduce strategic dependency through European sourcing wherever possible. Europe still benefits from companies involved in silicon extraction, such as Ferroglobe, and refining, such as Wacker Chemie. Start-ups are also emerging to bring the entire supply chain back to Europe: ReSilicon for silicon refining, and Sunwafe for ingots and wafers. We hope to offer fully EU-made modules as soon as possible.

What would you consider a healthy balance between domestic European solar manufacturing and imports from China?

A healthy balance would mean that Europe has sufficient domestic production to protect its strategic interests, maintain industrial know-how and support deployment in times of geopolitical or supply-chain disruption. Imports can remain part of the market, but they should complement European production rather than replace it.

The EU’s objective of having at least 40% of deployed PV made in Europe provides a useful benchmark.

Complete decoupling from China is not realistic in the short term, particularly given China's dominance in polysilicon and upstream manufacturing. Europe must start by protecting a share of the PV market, even if it is small at first, to allow manufacturing to be reshored.

What would need to happen in the European market for you to commit to a second production line or another gigafactory?

We would need two conditions: a strong IAA that creates a dedicated market for European-made PV components, and visibility on this addressable market. A second production line or factory would be considered once the Hambach plant is financed, operational and demonstrating that European manufacturing can compete at scale.

Have you already identified potential locations for additional manufacturing facilities, either in France or elsewhere in Europe?

Our immediate priority is to deliver the Hambach project. Any decision on a new plant will depend on market demand, public policy, infrastructure, financing and the performance of the first factory.

If European-made solar panels remain more expensive than imported alternatives, who should ultimately pay the difference?

The IAA focuses on two main market segments: public procurement and national auctions. Many PV projects are being developed with government support. The main aim is to channel this funding towards projects that use European-made panels.

It will be more expensive at first. Governments should provide targeted and temporary support to correct the structural disadvantages created by subsidies, dumping and externalities in international markets. However, there will also be some rewards, mainly through the creation of local jobs and additional tax revenues for governments.

The additional cost will be relatively low, however, as PV modules account for only 10% to 15% of a project's CAPEX. The impact of using European-made PV panels will be lower than that of the increase in financing costs we have seen in recent months.

What will be your main priorities during your first 12 months as CEO?

My priorities will be closely connected. First, securing strong and protective European regulation to create a market for our products. Second, finalising the industrial design, technology partnerships and supply chain. Third, converting customer interest into bankable commercial agreements. Finally, preparing the next fundraising round for the construction of the first buildings.

data.title: Anthropic shares fall 6% in pre-market trading after blockbuster debut amid global selloff over AI fears
data.description:
Shares of Anthropic, the maker of Claude AI, fell more than 6 percent in pre-market trading on November 20, giving back a part of the gains made during its blockbuster Wall Street debut a day earlier.

Anthropic shares were trading at $91 apiece, down 6.35 percent, as of 2:50 pm IST on November 20. The stock had closed its first trading session on the Nasdaq at $97.17 on Thursday, November 19, after surging 17.07 percent from its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.

The decline came amid concerns over intensifying competition in the artificial intelligence (AI) market after reports emerged that Apple was developing its own autonomous AI agent. The move could put Apple in more direct competition with AI developers such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta Platforms in the rapidly expanding market for autonomous AI tools.

The weakness in Anthropic shares also came against the backdrop of a broad sell-off in US equities. On Thursday, all three major US stock indices ended sharply lower, with technology and AI-linked stocks facing considerable selling pressure.

Despite the latest decline, Anthropic shares were still trading around 9.6 percent above their IPO price, indicating that the stock had retained most of its listing-day gains.

Anthropic made history on November 19 by raising approximately $81.34 billion through its IPO, making it the largest stock market debut on record and surpassing the previous record set by SpaceX.

The company priced its shares at $83 apiece, above the initially indicated price range of $70-$78. Its shares opened at $111.50 on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT, marking a premium of around 34 percent over the IPO price.

J. SMART & CO. (CONTRACTORS) PLC ANNOUNCES TODAY, FRIDAY 20 NOVEMBER 2026, ITS FULL YEAR RESULTS FOR THE YEAR TO 31st JULY 2026

The information contained within this announcement is deemed to constitute inside information as stipulated under the Market Abuse Regulations (EU) No. 596/2014. Upon the publication of this announcement, this inside information is now considered to be in the public domain.

CHAIRMAN’S REVIEW

ACCOUNTS

Group profit for the year before tax including an unrealised surplus in revalued property and a surplus in revalued financial assets was £2,416,000 compared with £6,868,000 last year.

As in previous years, our view is that disregarding the movement in the revaluation of the commercial property and financial assets provides a truer reflection of the Group’s performance, which we refer to as underlying profit.  The underlying loss before tax for the year was £184,000, compared with last year’s figure of a profit of £866,000, as detailed in note 10 to the financial statements.

The Board is recommending a Final Dividend of 2.29p, making a total of 3.25p.

TRADING ACTIVITIES

Group Profit decreased this financial year, as the value of the commercial property portfolio did not rise as significantly as the previous year.

Underlying profit before tax decreased this year to a loss due to poor performances in some of our subsidiary companies and lack of turnover causing overheads to erode profit.

Trading margins continue to be affected by the increases in the cost of construction materials and delays to construction programmes caused by issues with infrastructure utility and statutory approvals.

Whilst the affordable housing contract at Rosyth has now been agreed this was after the financial year end.  Therefore, there continued to be a lack of contract work in the housing association sector.

Sales at Winchburgh, Canal Quarter have nearly completed, but the prolonged sales period and associated holding costs have adversely affected the profit of this development.

The first sale at the private house development at Rosyth took place after the end of the financial year end.  Sales and reservations, to date, have been at a better than expected level.  However, due to the continuing economic issues in the UK, including the recent interest rate rise, exacerbated by the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, it remains to be seen how consumer confidence in private housing will affect sales going forward.

The industrial development at Inchmuir Park, Bathgate has now just completed.  However, due to inexplicable delays with utility infrastructure installations, completion was substantially later than anticipated.  The elongated nature of the programme has already reduced profitability.  Interest is initially promising, albeit no tenants have been secured as yet.

As mentioned in the Interim Report, we entered into a new Joint Venture Company, Smart (Manse1) Limited, with Manse (Smart 1) LLP.  Planning permission has now been granted for the industrial development at McNeil Drive, Eurocentral, North Lanarkshire for two new units of 80,000sq.ft. and 120,000sq.ft..  The intention is to secure all other necessary consents to enable construction to commence and speculatively develop the units, subject to obtaining funding.

Progress is being made with obtaining all necessary consents at Axis Point, Duloch Park, Dunfermline, the second industrial site mentioned in the Interim Report.  A decision will be made on whether development will commence in due course.

The value of our commercial property portfolio increased again this financial year, although not at the marked level as last year.  As predicted in the Interim Report, this was wholly due to continued rental growth, with investment yields remaining mainly static and in some instances getting weaker.

FUTURE PROSPECTS

The build contract for the affordable housing at Primrose Lane, Rosyth is the only external build contract we have at present.  The prospects of further external contract work are slim.

We had hoped to be able to report one of our residential developments for new build private rent, but the lack of clarity in the detail of the Housing (Scotland) Bill, the political uncertainty in Scotland and high build costs for flatted residential developments have all thwarted this for now.

There will be more private housing sales this year than the previous reported year.

Apart from the commercial developments already mentioned, it is hoped that the second phase of Gartcosh Business Park will commence in early 2027 through our joint venture company with Fusion Assets Limited, Gartcosh Estates LLP.

We expect letting and rental levels to remain steady in the industrial stock in our commercial property portfolio, with some rental growth.  We are experiencing limited voids in our office properties with rental growth static.  It has recently been reported by industry experts that prime yields in commercial property are starting to soften.  This may have a negative effect on the overall value of our portfolio in the next reporting year.

Therefore, it may be that we make both a headline and an underlying loss in the year to 31st July 2027.  This profit erosion will be due to a drop in commercial property values, limited external contracts and the continuing increases in material costs.

DAVID W SMART

Construction revenue in the year has decreased overall due to the progress of contracts in the year and number of private house sales in the year.

Work on the social housing contract at our Clovenstone development, being the 24 flats for Prospect Community Housing was completed in October 2025 and handed over to the housing association.  The work on the private housing at this development had also progressed throughout the year and was completed in November 2025.  Of the 45 private dwelling flats 15 had been sold in the prior financial year, and a remaining 30 flats were sold in this financial year to social housing providers.

Sales continue to be made at our private housing development at Canal View, Winchburgh albeit at a slower pace than hoped mainly due to the continuing uncertainties in the housing market.  In the year to 31st July 2026 we sold 13 properties, giving a total sold of 59 as at 31st July 2026 out of a total of 64 dwellings in the development.  Post year end we have sold a further 2 dwellings, leaving 3 unsold as yet at the development.  The remaining dwellings were written down in the year by £434,000 to reflect the anticipated net sale value.

Construction at our private housing development at Primrose Grange, Rosyth continued throughout the year.  The development consists of 107 houses over a phased construction programme.  Marketing of the first phase of the development was launched in the year and the 2 showhouses and sales office opened.  Interest has been promising and post year end we have sold 7 houses and have reservations for a further 4 houses.

Alongside the private housing development at Primrose Grange there is also a contract for 36 new energy efficient homes for Fife Council.  Construction commenced on site in August 2026.

Our civil engineering subsidiary, Thomas Menzies (Builders) Limited, has seen an increase in revenue of £352,000 being an increase of 10%.  However, the level of revenue generated by this subsidiary is insufficient to cover its overheads and therefore a loss was suffered by this company albeit at a lower level than the previous year.

Construction material costs continue to remain high for various reasons, including global unrest, inflation rate increases and the overall demand for goods and services causing increases in material and labour costs.  The Group continues to monitor costs on construction contracts, with the finance and surveyor teams liaising to ensure accurate recording of cost to contracts and monitoring of actual costs against anticipated costs and anticipated revenue to ensure projects remain on course and reviewing the impact on future costs to complete contracts.  The Directors continue to fully appraise contracts, at various stages, prior to acceptance to ascertain the likely outcome of the contract.   These appraisals are conducted prior to land bank acquisitions, commencement of construction and then during the lifetime of the contract to its completion.

Overheads continue to remain relatively constant in nature over time,  however they have increased in monetary terms due to inflationary increases.  The Directors do continue to monitor these with a view to achieving any savings on costs where possible.  With our revenue levels the recoverability of overhead is difficult.

The increased material construction costs together with increased labour costs has resulted in margins being reduced and the impact on the recoverability of overheads incurred by the Group has resulted in the operating loss incurred in the year.

Overall revenue for investment properties has increased in the year by 9%.  Rental income has increased by 6% due to rental growth throughout the portfolio,  mainly within our industrial properties, and increased occupancy.  Recoverability of rental income continues to remain high and the Group has suffered little in the way of defaulting tenants.

Income from service charges and insurance receivable varies from year to year depending on actual expenditure incurred in the year, overall in the year there has been an increase of 8% in this income.

There were no disposals of investment properties in the year.  Work continued at the speculative industrial development at Whitehill Industrial Estate, Bathgate which consists of four terraces of industrial units of 14,657 square feet each.  As at the year-end completion at the development had almost been completed, with service connections being the remaining work to be done.   Marketing of this development will commence once the development is fully completed.

Other additions to the investment property portfolio, occurred in our new subsidiary company, Smart (Manse 1) Limited.  This company acquired land at McNeil Drive, Eurocentral, North Lanarkshire.  Planning for two industrial / distribution units of 80,000 and 120,000 square feet was applied for and granted in the year.  As yet no construction of these units has commenced.

This year the Group has earned a surplus on the revaluation of investment property portfolio of £2,238,000, due to combined  improvement in yields and increased rental income.

Although there has been a significant decrease in operating profit compared to the previous year this is due to the surplus on revaluation of investment property portfolio recognised in the years, if this was to be excluded then the Group has earned an operating profit of £2,544,000 compared to £2,529,000 in the previous year, which is consistent over the two years.

Income from our financial assets has increased from that of the previous year.  There were a number of acquisitions in the year to our portfolio of financial assets along with a number of disposals on which the Group achieved a profit of £36,000.    Improvements in the world financial markets resulted in a surplus of £362,000 on the fair value of our financial assets being recorded for the year.

The share of the results in our Joint Ventures is a profit of £29,000.  In the current year the only trading joint venture was St Andrews 1413 Limited.  This company provides high quality student accommodation, which outwith university term time is available for short term holiday lets.  Occupancy for the student lets has been and continues to be fully let and the occupancy for the first year of holiday lets was encouraging.

Our net bank position, which comprises monies held on deposit, cash and cash equivalents and the netting of our bank overdraft has decreased in the year.  This is due to the cash outflow on acquisitions of the investment properties in the year either through own work capitalised or outright acquisition.  We have incurred various other inflows and outflows relating to sale proceeds from sales of our private housing and expenditure on construction activities of the housing.  Overall, the Group continues to be net debt-free.

The Group’s net assets have increased by £3,003,000, the main impact being the profits earned in the year, the movement in the Group’s pension scheme surplus of £6,257,000, the acquisitions of investment properties and the accounting for share buy backs and dividends paid to shareholders in the year.

PRINCIPAL RISKS AND UNCERTAINTIES

The principal risks and uncertainties faced by the Group and the mitigating factors taken by the Group against these risks are detailed below. The principal risks noted below are not all of the risks faced by the Group but are those risks which the Group perceives as those which could have a significant impact on the Group’s performance and future prospects.

Area of principal risk or uncertainty and impact

Mitigating actions and controls

By focusing external construction activities in the social housing sector, which is a competitive market, failure to win new contracts would impact on our volume of work and therefore the workforce required by the Group.

•     Maintain long-term relationships with social housing providers, resulting from high standards of service, quality and post construction care thus giving the Group an advantage over other builders when contracts are awarded on criteria other than cost only.

•     Identify potential build sites or include the provider within private housing developments in relation to the element of affordable housing required.

•     When workload is reduced workforce can be diverted to the Group’s own commercial and private residential developments.

•     Continue to acquire land for development for either private housing developments or for resale to social housing providers as part of a construction contract.

•     Develop new areas of construction activities.

•     Develop new joint venture opportunities.

Decline in home buyer confidence, due to bank interest rates, availability of affordable mortgages and cost of living crisis resulting in stalling of private house sales.

•     Building developments in popular residential areas.

•     Building high quality specification homes with attention to detail which sets them apart from other new build homes and therefore makes them more attractive to buyers.

•     Building a range of homes within a development thus providing choice to buyers.

•     Programming commencement of new build housing projects to market conditions.

•     Providing sales incentives.

•     Considering the letting of built homes at market rates.

Social housing sector and the housing market in general is highly competitive with tight margins.

•     We are an ‘all trades’ contractor who employs our own personnel in all basic building trades who are supervised by site agents who are long serving employees of the Group and who have been promoted through their trades, thus ensuring control of labour costs on contracts.

•     We have invested heavily in plant and the maintenance thereof and therefore limit our costs on contracts by utilising own plant as opposed to incurring higher costs of hiring plant.

•     Subcontractors employed by the Group are specialists in their fields and in the main subcontractors have previously been used by the Group therefore quality of work and reliability is known.

•     In house architectural technicians and surveyors provide pre-contract design advice to resolve potential technical problems with the build and therefore potential costs.

•     Detailed appraisals of contract pre-land acquisition and pre-construction.

Reduction in rental demand for investment properties may result in a fall in property valuations.

•     Only commence speculative developments after careful assessment of the market.

•     Continue to invest in property sectors which are robust.

•     Restricting our operations to the central belt of Scotland being the area of the country with which we are most familiar.

•     Continually maintain and refurbish existing properties to retain existing tenants and attract new tenants and improvements to our properties for improved economic and climate efficiencies.

•     Provide necessary financial incentives to retain existing tenants at end of current leases and attract new tenants.

Reduction in demand for UK real estate from investors may result in a fall in valuations within our investment property portfolio, this could result in delays in investment decisions which could impact on our activities.

•     The Directors regularly review the property market to ascertain if changes in the overall market present specific risks or opportunities to the Group.

•     Restricting our operations to the central belt of Scotland being the area of the country with which we are most familiar.

Political events and policies result in uncertainty until final decisions have been made and the impact of decisions are known, this could result in delays in investment decisions which could impact on our activities.  Including Local Government processes slowing down our ability to commence new building projects.

•     Before any decisions are taken by the Directors in any area of the Group’s activities the level of uncertainty and range of potential outcomes arising from political events and policies are considered.

•     Monitor Government guidelines and new legislations announcements to ensure the Group remains up to date with legislation.

•     Continue to pursue contacts at Local Government to obtain necessary consents and planning approval.

Reduction of financial resources.

•       Ensure resources are not over committed and only undertake commercial and private housing developments after due consideration of the financial impact on the Group’s financial resources.

•       Build up resources to ensure the Group has sufficient finance for working capital requirements and financing of commercial and private housing developments.

•       Spread cash reserves over several banks taking account of the strength of the bank and interest rates attainable.

•       Invest resources in equities also taking account of the security of the investment and the yields attainable.

Failure to evolve business practices and operations in response to climate change.

•       Continue to monitor all requirements relating to the construction industry in relation to improvements in buildings to ensure they comply with current and emerging requirements.

•       Review of designs for new buildings to ensure they are as energy efficient as possible.

•       Procurement of building materials from sustainable sources.

•       Investment in energy saving measures within our investment property portfolio.

•       Establishment of Sustainability Committee to develop the Group’s sustainability strategy with the commitment to reduce the Group’s carbon emissions in line with science-based carbon reduction targets.

•       Employ the services of external specialists and consultants for their expertise.

Unforeseen national and global events including world conflicts and natural disasters.

•  Establish strong relationships with suppliers and subcontractors to ascertain impact on their potential supply chains.

•  Build up financial resources to ensure the Group has sufficient funds for future working capital requirements.

•  Establish continuity plans for all areas of operations.

Impact of cost of living crisis, increased inflation and bank interest rates.

•  Retain strong control over costs on construction contracts.

•  Remunerate onsite and office based employees with competitive rates of pay and benefits.

Failure to comply with Laws and Regulations, including Employment Law, Health & Safety and building regulations.

•  Group policies established and training for staff thereon

•  Periodic review and update of Group policies

•  Use of external specialists to ensure compliance with laws and regulations

IT systems failures and security breaches.

•  Inhouse IT function established with external specialists also used

•  Review and update systems, security and contingency plans

•  Cyber insurance in place

Emerging Risks

The Group faces a number of emerging risks which could have a significant impact on the Group’s performance and future prospects.  These risks are discussed by the Directors and appropriate actions taken to mitigate these risks as soon as they are considered to be a principal risk of the Group.

GENERAL INFORMATION

J. Smart & Co. (Contractors) PLC which is the ultimate Parent Company of the J. Smart & Co. (Contractors) PLC Group is a public limited company registered in Scotland, incorporated in the United Kingdom and listed on the London Stock Exchange.

BASIS OF PREPARATI0N

The financial information in this announcement has been extracted from the Group’s Annual Report and Statement of Accounts for the year to 31st July 2026 and is prepared in accordance with UK-adopted international accounting standards in conformity with the requirements of the Companies Act 2006.  Whilst the financial information included in this preliminary announcement has been computed in accordance with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), this announcement does not itself contain sufficient information to comply with IFRS and the financial information set out does not constitute the Company or Groups statutory accounts for the years to 31st July 2026 or 31st July 2025.

The statutory consolidated accounts for the year to 31st July 2026 have been reported on by the Independent Auditor, their report was unqualified and did not draw attention to any matters by way of emphasis and it does not contain a statement under S498 (2) or S498 (3) of the Companies Act 2006.  The statutory consolidated accounts for the year to 31st July 2026 will be delivered to the Registrar of Companies following the Company’s Annual General Meeting.

The financial information for the year to 31st July 2025 is derived from the statutory accounts for that year which were submitted to the Registrar of Companies and upon which the Company’s auditor provided an unqualified audit report.  The audit report did not include a reference to any matters to which the auditor drew attention by way of emphasis without qualifying its report and did not contain a statement under S498 (2) or S498 (3) of the Companies Act 2006.

STANDARDS, AMENDMENTS TO STANDARDS AND INTERPRETATIONS EFFECTIVE IN THE YEAR TO 31st JULY 2026

The following new standards and amendments to standards and interpretations relevant to the Group have been issued by the International Accounting Standards Board and are mandatory for the first time for the financial year to 31st July 2026:

•  IAS 21 (amended): The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates

The above amendment to the standard has had no significant impact on the Group’s financial statements.

NEW STANDARDS, AMENDMENTS TO STANDARDS AND INTERPRETATIONS NOT YET APPLIED

There have been no new standards, amendments to standards and interpretations relevant to the Group that have been issued by the International Accounting Standards Board but are not yet effective for the Group at the date of these financial statements.

IFRS 18: Presentation and Disclosures in Financial Statements is replacing IAS 1: Presentation of Financial Statements and will be effective for the Group as from the accounting year ending 31st July 2028.  This standard will result in changes to the presentation of the Income Statement to disclose the required mandatory subtotals and the reporting of financial performance and additional disclosures within the notes to the accounts.

BASIS OF PREPARATION

The financial statements have been prepared under the historical cost convention except where the measurement of balances at fair value is required as noted below for investment properties, financial assets and assets held by the defined benefit pension scheme.

The accounting policies set out below have been consistently applied to all periods presented in these financial statements.

The preparation of financial statements requires management to make estimates and assumptions concerning   the future that may affect the application of accounting policies and the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and income and expenses. Management believes that the estimates and assumptions used in the preparation of these financial statements are reasonable. However, actual outcomes may differ from those anticipated.

GOING CONCERN

The financial statements have been prepared on a going concern basis. The Directors have prepared a number of cashflows scenarios taking account of future trading activities around construction projects in hand and anticipated projects, land acquisitions, rental income, investment property acquisitions and disposals and other capital expenditure.  In each scenario reviewed by the Directors the Group remains cash positive with no reliance on external funding and therefore remains net debt-free. The net assets of the Group are £133,606,000 at 31st July 2026 and the Group’s net current assets amount to £18,151,000.  The Directors have also taken account of the impact of climate changes on the activities of the Group.  Taking all of the information the Directors currently have they are of the opinion that the Company and Group are well placed to manage their financial and business risks and have a reasonable expectation that the Company and Group have adequate financial resources to continue in operational existence for a period of at least twelve months from the date of approval of these financial statements and therefore consider the adoption of the going concern basis as appropriate for the preparation of these financial statements.

CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES AND JUDGEMENTS

ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES

INVESTMENT PROPERTIES

Investment properties are revalued annually by the Directors in accordance with the RICS Valuation Standards. The valuations are subjective due to, among other factors, the individual nature of the property, its location and the expected future rental income. As a result, the valuation of the Group’s investment property portfolio incorporated into the financial statements is subject to a degree of uncertainty and is made on the basis of assumptions which may prove to be inaccurate, particularly in periods of volatility or low transaction flow in the property market.

The assumptions used by the Directors are market standard assumptions in accordance with the RICS Valuation Standards and include matters such as tenure and tenancy details, ground conditions of the properties and their structural conditions, prevailing market yields and comparable market conditions. If any of the assumptions used by the Directors prove to be incorrect this could result in the valuation of the Group’s investment property portfolio differing from the valuation incorporated into the financial statements and the difference could have a material effect on the financial statements.

RETIREMENT BENEFIT OBLIGATION

The valuation of the retirement benefit obligation is dependent upon a series of assumptions, mainly discount rates, mortality rates, investment returns, salary inflation and the rate of pension increases, which are determined after taking expert advice from the Group’s Actuary. If different assumptions were used then this could materially affect the results disclosed in the financial statements.

ACCOUNTING JUDGEMENTS

CASH AND CASH EQUIVALENTS

As the Group has a pooling arrangement with its bankers and the bank has been granted guarantees and letters of offset by certain members of the Group in favour of the bank on account of all these members as continuing security for all monies, obligations and liabilities owing or incurred to the bank then, for the purposes of the Statement of Cash Flows and the calculation of cash and cash equivalents, the bank overdraft is netted against positive bank balances.  The Directors consider the bank balances whether positive or negative to be part of the Group’s ordinary working capital cycle.  In accordance with IAS 7: Statement of Cash Flows, the Directors deem the bank overdraft to be cash and cash equivalents and not borrowings as this balance is being used for working capital and other trading activities.  Overall the Group is not allowed to be in an overdrawn bank position in the pooling arrangement, however individual companies within the arrangement may have an overdrawn bank balance.  The Group and Company present positive and negative bank balances separately on the face of the Statement of Financial Position and do not offset these balances for presentation purposes as there is not legal right to offset.  Companies not in the pooling arrangement do not have an overdraft facility and therefore their bank balances cannot be overdrawn.

RECOVERABILITY OF WORK IN PROGRESS

The Group considers contract performance to ensure appropriate revenue recognition. Future revenue, contract performance and stage of completion of contracts are considered and loss provisions determined and recognised where necessary. Both costs and revenues may require to be revised as future events unfold and uncertainties are resolved, which would have a direct impact on overall performance of these contracts.

The Group takes account of all anticipated losses on work in progress contacts at the year end and therefore considers that the value of work in progress included in the financial statements is recoverable.

DEFINED BENEFIT RETIREMENT PENSION SCHEME SURPLUS

The Group has concluded that the trust deed relating to the defined benefit retirement pension scheme grants the unconditional right to any surplus of the scheme on the full settlement of the scheme liabilities to the Group and therefore has concluded that any surplus on the scheme can be incorporated into the Group and Company financial statements. Advice on the Group’s right to a surplus arising on the pension scheme was sought in the year to 31st July 2022 from a firm of lawyers who specialise in this area.  Their advice was that the Group had an unconditional right to the surplus based on the original Trust Deed and Deed of Variation and therefore the full surplus arising on the calculation thereof under IAS 19 (amended): Employee Benefits should be accounted for in the financial statements.  The Group sought and received confirmation for the year to 31st July 2026 from the same firm of lawyers that there had been no change in their advice.

Valuation Process

The Group’s investment properties are valued by David W Smart, MRICS, who is a Director of the Parent Company, on the basis of fair value, in accordance with the RICS Valuation – Global Standards, incorporating the International Valuations Standards, and RICS Professional Standards UK January 2014 (revised April 2015).

Investment properties, excluding ongoing developments, are valued using the investment method of valuation. This approach involves applying capitalisation yields to current and estimated future rental streams and then allowing for voids arising from vacancies and rent free periods and associated running costs. The capitalisation yields and rental values are based on comparable property and leasing transactions in the market, using the valuers’ professional judgement and market observations. Other factors taken into account in the valuations include the tenure of the property, tenancy details and ground and structural conditions.

In the case of ongoing developments, the approach applied is the residual method of valuation, which is the same as the investment method, as described above, with a deduction for all costs necessary to complete the  development, together with a further allowance for remaining risk.

data.title: Nasdaq Set for Fresh Decline as AI Selloff Intensifies
data.description:
By Joe Stonor

Global stocks sold off and Treasurys strengthened as investor confidence in the artificial-intelligence trade showed signs of cracking.

Nasdaq futures dropped 1.15%, extending sharp falls from the last session. S&P 500 futures fell 0.5%, while contracts tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.1%. Major U.S. indexes are on track for their worst week since the announcement of President Trump's Liberation Day tariffs upended global trade in April 2025.

Anthropic's record-breaking IPO failed to stem heavy selling across global stocks. Chip makers, tech giants and cloud-computing stocks weakened in U.S. premarket trade after heavy selling across Asian tech names. The memory chip-dominated Kospi closed 5.2% lower, while Japan's Nikkei also fell more than 5%. Taiwan's Taiex sank 6.2%, bringing its weekly loss to more than 17%--its worst week since 1990.

The selling bled to European stocks, too. ASML, the continent's most valuable stock, fell more than 5% as a basket of the continent's tech stocks opened 3% lower. The continent-wide Stoxx 600 was 1.2% lower.

Demand for Anthropic's IPO is focusing attention on the sustainability of the AI investment buildout while also draining liquidity from the broader market, said Roger Lee, head of equity strategy at Cavendish.

The gloominess in stock market sentiment comes despite fresh declines for oil. Benchmark Brent crude contracts dropped around 1.25% to $90.85 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate contracts fell 1.7% to trade around $81.80 a barrel. The U.S. Energy Information Administration said Thursday that oil shipments through major Middle Eastern shipping routes increased 19% in the third quarter.

Lower oil prices and an investor flight to safety combined to strengthen Treasurys. Ten-year yields fell back below 5.000%, while two-year yields dropped 6 basis points to 4.720%. Thirty-year yields fell 3.1 basis points to trade around 5.370%.

Metals prices continued to sell off, with gold tumbling close to 3% at $3,580 a troy ounce. The dollar held near multimonth highs, while bitcoin rebounded slightly but remained near July lows, hovering just below $62,000.

For the day ahead, macro watchers will look to Michigan's consumer sentiment index for November, and to Federal Reserve speakers including Christopher Waller.

data.title: Zloty slips as Fed hike fears boost dollar; Moody's Hungary review in focus
data.description:
Most Central European currencies were under pressure on Friday as geopolitical risks and expectations of further Fed interest rate hikes curbed risk appetite, while investors awaited Moody's review of Hungary's sovereign rating later in the day.

The Polish zloty hit a three-year low late on Thursday, driven by what analysts described as expectations of "aggressive" Fed rate hikes and a lack of progress towards peace in Ukraine.

Markets are pricing in a 25-basis-point US rate hike in December as near-certain, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

The zloty will remain primarily influenced by the strength of the US dollar, weakening investor demand for emerging market assets and a selloff in global equity markets, PKO BP analysts wrote in a note.

"Given this external environment — which is unfavourable for the zloty — the EUR/PLN and USD/PLN exchange rates may end Friday’s trading session near 4.44 and 4.05, respectively."

The zloty fell 0.35% to 4.4480 per euro by 0904 GMT, while the Hungarian forint was stable at 372.50.

Analysts expect Moody's to leave Hungary's Baa2 rating and negative outlook unchanged.

"HUF led regional losses (EUR/HUF: +1.2%), sliding for a third day and crossing 370 per euro, as the central bank signalled a potential rate cut next month," analysts at Morgan Stanley said.

Hungary's central bank left its base rate unchanged at 5.5% (HUINT=ECI) on Tuesday, as expected, but indicated it could have greater scope to ease monetary policy when it updates its inflation forecasts in December.

Stock markets in the region fell in the wake of a selloff on global bourses. Warsaw was down 2.2% and Budapest lost 1.3%.
